vignette:
She remembers the night clearly, even though she has tried to forget. It was almost a year ago, just after she started working the night shift at the call center. She was twenty-one, newly married, and still learning how to balance her life with her husband's schedule. The assault happened on the short walk from the bus stop to her apartment-a route she had taken dozens of times before. A man she did not know followed her from the station, grabbed her arm, and pulled her behind a low wall near the construction site. It was over in minutes. He left without saying a word. She walked the rest of the way home in a daze, showered, and told no one.

Now she sits in the therapy office on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands folded tightly in her lap. She is twenty-two. She still works the same night shift, but she takes a different bus and walks a longer, brighter route home. Every time she passes a man walking behind her, her shoulders tense and her breathing quickens. She checks her phone repeatedly, pretending to talk to someone so that no one will approach. When she gets home, she locks the door three times, then checks the windows. Her husband, who works a day job, sometimes wakes up when she comes in. He asks if she's okay. She says she's tired.

She cannot bring herself to tell him what happened. She knows it wasn't her fault, but the word fault sits in her stomach like a heavy stone. She thinks he would look at her differently-maybe with pity, maybe with doubt. He is a kind man, but they come from a culture where a woman's purity is still tied to her worth. She has imagined the conversation a hundred times, the words forming and dissolving on her tongue. Instead, she avoids being touched at night. She tells him she's too tired from the calls. When he presses close, she freezes, her body going rigid until he gives up. She hates the look of hurt on his face, but she cannot explain.

At work, she keeps her voice steady. The call center is a sea of cubicles, headsets, and fluorescent lights. She handles customer complaints about phone bills and service outages. Most callers are angry before they even speak. She learned to absorb it, to smile into the headset. But now every raised voice makes her jump. Every male caller with a deep, commanding tone triggers a hot flush of panic that starts in her chest and spreads to her hands. She has learned to mute her microphone for fifteen seconds at a time, just to breathe. Sometimes she dissociates completely-she hears herself saying the scripted lines, but she feels like she is watching from above the ceiling tiles. When she hangs up, she cannot remember what the customer said.

She has nightmares two or three times a week. In the dreams, the man is faceless but she feels his weight, his breath. She wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and lies perfectly still until the clock's red numbers become clear. She does not cry. Crying feels like admitting that it is still happening. She cut her hair short last month because she could not stand the feeling of it brushing the back of her neck-it reminded her of his hand. She stopped eating dinner because her stomach clenches every evening around the time the assault happened.

Her husband asked her last week if she was seeing someone else. She told him no and walked out of the room. She wants to tell him, she really does. But the words feel too heavy. So she carries them alone, night after night, sitting in the break room with cold coffee, staring at the wall. She has stopped laughing. She does not remember the last time she felt something close to joy. She is not sad, exactly-she is hollow, like a bell that has been struck too hard and now only hums with a low, empty vibration.

This is how she lives now: planning her routes, avoiding eye contact with strangers, muting her microphone, locking the doors, and waiting for the next wave to hit. She does not know that it has a name. She only knows that every day is a negotiation with a man she cannot see, and that the night shift no longer feels like just a shift-it feels like a sentence.
